title: Learn by Doing: Control Structures
lead: The topic sat as a paper: its objective questions, then every past question on decisions, loops and dry runs, each with its model answer, and the method taught from nothing.
intro:
Part A is the objective questions on this topic, the largest group in the bank. Part B is past questions only, and this topic carries the most of them: every dry run, every debug snippet built on a loop, and the number theory programs.

The dry run is the cheapest question on the paper and the one most often lost, because it is done in the head instead of in a table.

lockin.big: "A dry run is a table, one column per variable and one row per pass. Never do it in your head."
lockin.sub: A for loop when the count is known, a while when it is not, a do-while when the body must run at least once. break leaves the loop, continue skips to the next pass.

methodFrames.teach:
Three loops, and the exam asks you to tell them apart and to convert between them. A for loop when you know how many times, a while when you do not, a do-while when the body must run at least once.

public class Loops {    public static void main(String[] args) {        for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) System.out.print(i + " ");        System.out.println();        int j = 5;        while (j >= 1) { System.out.print(j + " "); j--; }        System.out.println();        int k = 10;        do { System.out.print("ran once "); k++; } while (k < 5);        System.out.println();    }}
Output1 2 3 4 5 
5 4 3 2 1 
ran once
methodFrames.ask: What do you expect each of these three to print?

methodFrames.teach:
The do-while is the one to notice: its condition was false from the start and the body still ran, because a do-while tests AFTER. That is a favourite objective question.

Converting a for into a while is on the paper: take the three parts out of the for and put them where they belong.

for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { ... }int i = 1;          // 1. the initialisation goes above the loopwhile (i <= 5) {    // 2. the condition goes in the while    ...    i++;            // 3. the update goes at the END of the body}
methodFrames.ask: If you put the update at the TOP of the while body instead of the bottom, what breaks?

methodFrames.check: The first pass uses the wrong value and the count is off by one.
methodFrames.teach:
The first pass uses the wrong value and the loop runs one fewer time. That is a planted error in a debug question, so check where the update sits every time.

Now the dry run, which is four marks on the 24/25 paper, three times over. The method is a table: one column per variable, one row per pass.

public class Trace {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int sum = 0;        for (int i = 1; i <= 7; i++) {            if (i % 2 == 0) continue;            if (i > 5) break;            sum += i;            System.out.println("i=" + i + " sum=" + sum);        }        System.out.println("final " + sum);    }}
Outputi=1 sum=1
i=3 sum=4
i=5 sum=9
final 9
methodFrames.ask: Trace this one on paper before you run it: what is the final sum?

methodFrames.teach: 9. The even numbers are skipped by continue, and break leaves the loop at i = 7 before it can be added. The two keywords are asked as a pair: continue skips the rest of this pass, break leaves the loop entirely.
methodFrames.ask: Now decisions. In an if-else-if ladder, why does the order of the tests matter?

methodFrames.check: It stops at the first test that is true, so a wide test placed early swallows everything.
methodFrames.teach:
Because the ladder stops at the first true test. A grade ladder must run from the highest boundary down, or a score of 90 matches a test for 45 and above and is graded wrongly.

public class Fall {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int level = 2;        switch (level) {            case 1: System.out.println("Bronze");            case 2: System.out.println("Silver");            case 3: System.out.println("Gold"); break;            default: System.out.println("unranked");        }    }}
OutputSilver
Gold
methodFrames.ask: A switch does the same job for exact values. What happens if you leave out a break inside it?

methodFrames.check: Silver and Gold, because the missing break falls through.
methodFrames.teach:
It falls through: execution carries on into the next case until it meets a break. Level 2 printed Silver AND Gold, because only the third case ends in a break. Deliberate fall through is used to group cases; accidental fall through is a planted error.

Note the rest of the rules: a switch works on int, char, String and enum, default catches everything else, and case labels must be constants.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, Question One, 10 marks

scenario.text:
[10 Marks]D. An Armstrong number (also called a narcissistic number) is a positive integer that is equal to the sum of its own digits, each raised to the power of the total number of digits in the number. For example, 153 is an Armstrong number because 1³ + 5³ + 3³ = 1 + 125 + 27 = 153.

i.    State the five outputs for this code (you can show your workings but make the answer bold)

ii.   Retain other things but change the For Loop to While loop and the While loops to For loops.

exam.problem: Write your answer to the question above in your book first. It carries 10 marks, so write one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Q1 d i · state the five outputs · 10 MARKS, PART ONE

The answer. Compute each digit cubed (all five are 3-digit numbers, so the power is 3):

nsum of digits3= n?Output
37027 + 343 + 0 = 370yes370 -> ARMSTRONG
37127 + 343 + 1 = 371yes371 -> ARMSTRONG
37227 + 343 + 8 = 378no372 -> NOT ARMSTRONG
40764 + 0 + 343 = 407yes407 -> ARMSTRONG
40864 + 0 + 512 = 576no408 -> NOT ARMSTRONG

The arithmetic: 33 = 27, 73 = 343, 03 = 0, 13 = 1, 23 = 8, 43 = 64, 83 = 512. Three of the five are Armstrong numbers, which is worth noticing: the examiner chose 370, 371 and 407 because they are the three three-digit Armstrong numbers next to each other, and 372 and 408 as near misses.

Code · confirmed by running the paper's own code · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class ArmstrongChecker {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] numbers = {370, 371, 372, 407, 408};        for (int idx = 0; idx < numbers.length; idx++) {            int n = numbers[idx], digits = 0, temp = n, sum = 0;            while (temp > 0) { digits++; temp /= 10; }            temp = n;            while (temp > 0) {                int d = temp % 10, power = 1;                for (int p = 0; p < digits; p++) power *= d;                sum += power;                temp /= 10;            }            System.out.println(n + " -> "                + (sum == n ? "ARMSTRONG" : "NOT ARMSTRONG"));        }    }}
Output370 -> ARMSTRONG
371 -> ARMSTRONG
372 -> NOT ARMSTRONG
407 -> ARMSTRONG
408 -> NOT ARMSTRONG
Q1 d ii · convert the loops · 10 MARKS, PART TWO

Read it precisely. The original has three loops:

LoopCurrentlyBecomes
the outer one over idxforwhile
counting the digitswhilefor
summing the powerswhilefor
the inner p loopforwhile

"The For Loop" (singular) is the outer one; "the While loops" (plural) are the two digit loops. The innermost p loop is also a for, so convert it too: the safest reading is that every for becomes a while and every while becomes a for. Apply Unit 4.6's recipe to each.

Code · every loop converted, same output · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class ArmstrongConverted {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] numbers = {370, 371, 372, 407, 408};        // FOR -> WHILE: init out, condition in, update at the bottom        int idx = 0;        while (idx < numbers.length) {            int n = numbers[idx], digits = 0, temp = n, sum = 0;            // WHILE -> FOR: no init needed, temp is the counter            for (; temp > 0; temp /= 10) {                digits++;            }            temp = n;            // WHILE -> FOR            for (; temp > 0; temp /= 10) {                int d = temp % 10, power = 1;                // FOR -> WHILE                int p = 0;                while (p < digits) {                    power *= d;                    p++;                }                sum += power;            }            System.out.println(n + " -> "                + (sum == n ? "ARMSTRONG" : "NOT ARMSTRONG"));            idx++;                      // the update, at the bottom        }    }}
Output370 -> ARMSTRONG
371 -> ARMSTRONG
372 -> NOT ARMSTRONG
407 -> ARMSTRONG
408 -> NOT ARMSTRONG

Identical output to the original. That is the test of a conversion: same program, different clothes.

Two points a marker looks for. The for (; temp > 0; temp /= 10) has an empty initialisation, which is legal and is the honest conversion: the original while had nothing to initialise, because temp already existed. Do not invent a variable to fill the slot. And idx++ sits at the bottom of the while body, which is Unit 4.6's step 3 and the one people forget: leave it out and the program runs forever.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, Question Two, 10 marks

scenario.text:
[10 marks]D. A perfect number is a positive integer that is equal to the sum of its own proper positive divisors (all divisors excluding the number itself). For example, 6 is perfect because 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. A number whose proper divisors sum to more than the number itself is called abundant, and one whose proper divisors sum to less than the number itself is called deficient.

i.    State the output for this code (no need to show workings)

ii.   Change the For loops to While loops

exam.answer:
Q2 d i · state the output · 10 MARKS, PART ONE

The answer: Perfect: 2, Abundant: 5, Deficient: 23

The reasoning, which is worth writing out because "no need to show workings" does not mean "do not check":

ClassCountWhich
Perfect26 (1+2+3 = 6) and 28 (1+2+4+7+14 = 28)
Abundant512 (16), 18 (21), 20 (22), 24 (36), 30 (42)
Deficient23everything else, including every prime, and 1

Two checks that catch mistakes. 2 + 5 + 23 = 30, so every number is classified exactly once. And 1 is deficient: its proper divisors sum to 0, because 1 has no proper divisor, and the loop for (div = 1; div < num; div++) never runs for num = 1. Forget that and you get 22, not 23.

Code · confirmed, with the classification printed · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class NumberClassifier {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int perfectCount = 0, abundantCount = 0, deficientCount = 0;        for (int num = 1; num <= 30; num++) {            int sum = 0;            for (int div = 1; div < num; div++) {                if (num % div == 0) sum += div;            }            if (sum == num) perfectCount++;            else if (sum > num) abundantCount++;            else deficientCount++;        }        System.out.println("Perfect: " + perfectCount + ", Abundant: " + abundantCount            + ", Deficient: " + deficientCount);        System.out.println("check: " + (perfectCount + abundantCount + deficientCount)            + " numbers classified");    }}
OutputPerfect: 2, Abundant: 5, Deficient: 23
check: 30 numbers classified
Code · q2 d ii · for loops converted to while loops · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class NumberClassifierWhile {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int perfectCount = 0, abundantCount = 0, deficientCount = 0;        int num = 1;                        // 1. init above        while (num <= 30) {                 // 2. condition            int sum = 0;            int div = 1;                    // the inner one too            while (div < num) {                if (num % div == 0) sum += div;                div++;                      // 3. update at the bottom            }            if (sum == num) perfectCount++;            else if (sum > num) abundantCount++;            else deficientCount++;            num++;                          // 3. update at the bottom        }        System.out.println("Perfect: " + perfectCount + ", Abundant: " + abundantCount            + ", Deficient: " + deficientCount);    }}
OutputPerfect: 2, Abundant: 5, Deficient: 23

Identical output, which is the whole test. Note int sum = 0; stays inside the outer loop: it must be reset for every number, and moving it out is the classic way to wreck this conversion. The recipe only moves the loop's own three parts; everything else stays exactly where it was, which is what "retain other things" means.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, Question Six, 12 marks

scenario.text:
(12 marks)A. Design and implement a program, using JOptionPane only for input and output, that classifies a single user-supplied positive integer N according to its digit pattern (Palindrome).

Definition: A number is a palindrome if it reads the same forwards and backwards (i.e. it is equal to its own digit-reversed value). For example, 4884 and 7 are palindromes; 4821 is not.

Constraints: The entire task must be implemented inside main() only, using loops and nested/chained if-else and/or switch logic. No arrays and no user-defined helper methods are permitted; everything must be inline.

i.    Using a loop built only on the % and / operators (no converting N to a String or array), compute, in the same loop:

•  the digit sum of N, and

•  the value of N with its digits reversed (e.g. for N = 4821, the reversed value is 1284).

ii.   Determine whether N is a palindrome by comparing N directly to the reversed value computed in step 1.

iii.  Inline in main() (not a separate method), determine whether the digit sum from step 1 is itself a prime number. Use a loop that tests divisibility only up to the square root of the digit sum.

iv.  Using nested/chained conditional logic, classify N into exactly one of the following categories, checked strictly in this priority order:

•  "PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM": if N is a palindrome AND its digit sum is prime

•  "PALINDROME": if N is a palindrome but its digit sum is not prime

•  "HARSHAD": if N is not a palindrome but N is exactly divisible by its own digit sum

•  "STANDARD": in every other case

v.   Display N, its digit sum, its reversed value, and its final classification in a single JOptionPane message dialog.

exam.problem: Write your answer to the question above in your book first. It carries 12 marks, so write one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Q6 a · classify a number by its digit pattern · 12 MARKS
  1. in one loop, built only on % and / (no converting N to a String or array), compute both the digit sum of N and N with its digits reversed;
  2. N is a palindrome if it equals its reversed value;
  3. inline, decide whether the digit sum is prime, testing divisibility only up to its square root;
  4. classify, strictly in this priority order: PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM (palindrome and sum prime), PALINDROME (palindrome, sum not prime), HARSHAD (not a palindrome, but N divides exactly by its digit sum), STANDARD otherwise;
  5. show N, its digit sum, its reversed value and its classification in a single dialog.
Must memorise · The digit loop, and the copy that saves it

Peeling digits off a number is three lines you should be able to write without thinking:

int digit = temp % 10;   takes the last digit
reversed = reversed * 10 + digit;   pushes it onto the right of the answer
temp = temp / 10;   drops the last digit

Loop while (temp > 0). Both answers fall out of one pass.

The line the marks hang on is int temp = n;. The loop destroys whatever it walks: temp ends at 0. Walk n itself and by step 2 there is nothing left to compare the reversed value against, and nothing left to divide in step 4. Copy it, consume the copy.

reversed * 10 + digit is worth a moment. Take 4821: the loop pulls 1, then 2, then 8, then 4. Start at 0, and each step shifts what you have one place left and drops the new digit into the units: 1, then 12, then 128, then 1284. The digits come off backwards, which is exactly why pushing them on in the order they arrive reverses the number.

MEMORY HOOK: % takes the last digit, / removes it. Every digit problem in this course is those two lines and a loop.

Teach · The square root test, without Math.sqrt

Part 3 says test divisibility only up to the square root of the digit sum. The clean way needs no square root at all:

boolean sumIsPrime = (digitSum >= 2);for (int f = 2; f * f <= digitSum; f++) {    if (digitSum % f == 0) { sumIsPrime = false; break; }}

f * f <= digitSum is "f is at most the square root of digitSum", squared on both sides. It stays in whole numbers, so there is no Math.sqrt, no double, and no floating-point comparison to get wrong at the boundary (Unit 3.6).

Why stopping at the square root is correct, not just faster. If digitSum = a * b, then a and b cannot both be above the square root, or their product would exceed digitSum. So every factor pairs with one at or below the square root. Find none there and there are none at all.

And the initialiser is the whole edge case. digitSum >= 2 is what makes 1 not prime and 0 not prime. The loop cannot help you: for digitSum = 1 it never runs, so whatever you started with survives. Start at true and the program declares 1 prime, and then N = 1 (a palindrome with digit sum 1) is misclassified. See the table below, last row.

Code · question six, part a · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.util.Scanner;public class PalindromeClassifier {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        int n = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());        // Step i: ONE loop, using only % and /, computing BOTH the digit sum and        // the reversed value. temp is consumed; n must survive for step ii.        int temp = n;        int digitSum = 0;        int reversed = 0;        while (temp > 0) {            int digit = temp % 10;            digitSum = digitSum + digit;            reversed = reversed * 10 + digit;            temp = temp / 10;        }        // Step ii: palindrome is a comparison against the ORIGINAL n.        boolean isPalindrome = (n == reversed);        // Step iii: is digitSum prime? Test factors only up to its square root.        boolean sumIsPrime = (digitSum >= 2);        for (int f = 2; f * f <= digitSum; f++) {            if (digitSum % f == 0) {                sumIsPrime = false;                break;            }        }        // Step iv: classify, in the paper's priority order.        String classification;        if (isPalindrome) {            if (sumIsPrime) {                classification = "PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM";            } else {                classification = "PALINDROME";            }        } else if (n % digitSum == 0) {            classification = "HARSHAD";        } else {            classification = "STANDARD";        }        // Step v: one dialog with all four facts.        String message = "N: " + n                       + "\nDigit sum: " + digitSum                       + "\nReversed: " + reversed                       + "\nClassification: " + classification;        System.out.println(message);    }}
OutputN: 4884
Digit sum: 24
Reversed: 4884
Classification: PALINDROME

4884 is the paper's own example. It is a palindrome, and 24 = 2 × 12 is not prime, so it is PALINDROME and not PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM. That is the priority order doing its job.

Code · the same statements, run over every case · SO THE TABLE IS REAL

This is not the exam answer: the question forbids helper methods and demands a single N. It is the identical block of statements with a loop around it, so that every row below is real output rather than someone's arithmetic.

import java.util.Scanner;// The SAME statements as the answer, with a loop around them, so that every row// of the table in this book is real output rather than someone's arithmetic.public class ClassifierBench {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        System.out.println("     N | sum | reversed | classification");        while (in.hasNextLine()) {            String line = in.nextLine();            if (line.isEmpty()) {                continue;            }            int n = Integer.parseInt(line);            int temp = n, digitSum = 0, reversed = 0;            while (temp > 0) {                int digit = temp % 10;                digitSum = digitSum + digit;                reversed = reversed * 10 + digit;                temp = temp / 10;            }            boolean isPalindrome = (n == reversed);            boolean sumIsPrime = (digitSum >= 2);            for (int f = 2; f * f <= digitSum; f++) {                if (digitSum % f == 0) {                    sumIsPrime = false;                    break;                }            }            String classification;            if (isPalindrome) {                classification = sumIsPrime ? "PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM" : "PALINDROME";            } else if (n % digitSum == 0) {                classification = "HARSHAD";            } else {                classification = "STANDARD";            }            System.out.printf("%6d | %3d | %8d | %s%n", n, digitSum, reversed,                classification);        }    }}
Output     N | sum | reversed | classification
  4884 |  24 |     4884 | PALINDROME
     7 |   7 |        7 | PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM
  4821 |  15 |     1284 | STANDARD
    21 |   3 |       12 | HARSHAD
   131 |   5 |      131 | PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM
     1 |   1 |        1 | PALINDROME

Six rows, and every branch of part 4 is exercised. 4884 and 4821 are the paper's own two examples and both come out as the paper says. 7 is its one-digit palindrome. 4821: the digit sum is 15 and 4821 = 15 × 321 + 6, so it is not a Harshad number either, and it falls to STANDARD. 1 is the row worth staring at: a palindrome whose digit sum is 1, and 1 is not prime, so PALINDROME. Get the initialiser wrong and this row alone would read PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM.

Trap · "Priority order" means else-if, not four ifs

Part 4 says checked strictly in this priority order and exactly one category. Both phrases point at the same structure: one chain, where reaching a test means every test above it already failed.

Write four independent ifs and a palindrome with a prime digit sum matches the first, then falls into the others too, and your single dialog reports whichever assignment landed last. The chain is what makes "exactly one" true, and it is also what makes HARSHAD's rule readable: HARSHAD never has to say "and is not a palindrome", because it is only ever reached when the palindrome test failed. The order does that work, which is precisely why the question fixes it (Unit 4.2).

Watch n % digitSum in the HARSHAD test. It is safe here only because N is a positive integer, so digitSum is at least 1 and never 0. Take that guarantee away and it throws ArithmeticException (Unit 3.6): a division by zero hiding in a remainder.

scenario.text: [4 marks]C. Dry run this code snippet with the following values: 3,4,5,7.

breakdown.answer:
GivenA method and four values to feed it.
Asked forA dry run, the lecturer's own word for tracing by hand and stating what comes out. Four values means four answers.
The marks4 marks, four values: one each. Show the trace, because a bare number cannot earn method marks if you slip.
WatchLook at the types before you compute anything. Both operands are int, so this is integer division, and that decides the whole answer.

exam.problem: Write your answer to the question above in your book first. It carries 4 marks, so write one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Q1 c · dry run sumseries with 3, 4, 5, 7 · 4 MARKS

The answer is 0. For all four values.

Must memorise · Four values, one answer, and that is the question

j and j + 1 are both int, so j / (j + 1) is integer division.

j is always smaller than j + 1. A smaller int divided by a larger int is always 0. Every term is 0. The sum is 0.

1/2 is 0. 2/3 is 0. 3/4 is 0. Not 0.5, 0.67, 0.75: 0, because integer division throws the remainder away (Unit 3.6). It does not round; it truncates.

Why the examiner gave you four values. Being handed 3, 4, 5 and 7 shouts "four different answers". It is bait. The four values are there so that you either notice the types once and answer all four in one line, or trace fractions by hand for ten minutes and write four confident wrong numbers.

MEMORY HOOK: int / int is an int. Before you trace any division, look at the two types. One double anywhere on top and the answer changes completely: 1.0 / 2 is 0.5.

Code · the paper's own method, run · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class SumSeriesTrace {    // exactly as the paper prints it    public static int sumSeries(int i) {        int sum = 0;        for (int j = 1; j <= i; j++) {            sum += j / (j + 1);        }        return sum;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println("sumSeries(3) = " + sumSeries(3));        System.out.println("sumSeries(4) = " + sumSeries(4));        System.out.println("sumSeries(5) = " + sumSeries(5));        System.out.println("sumSeries(7) = " + sumSeries(7));        System.out.println("and the terms themselves: 1/2 = " + (1 / 2)            + ", 2/3 = " + (2 / 3) + ", 3/4 = " + (3 / 4));        System.out.println("with a double on top:     1.0/2 = " + (1.0 / 2));    }}
OutputsumSeries(3) = 0
sumSeries(4) = 0
sumSeries(5) = 0
sumSeries(7) = 0
and the terms themselves: 1/2 = 0, 2/3 = 0, 3/4 = 0
with a double on top:     1.0/2 = 0.5

Four inputs, one answer. The last two lines are the whole explanation: every term really is 0, and the single change that would rescue the method is a double on top.

Dry run · How to write this up for 4 marks

Do not just write "0" four times. Show the trace for one value and generalise; that is what the marks are for.

sumSeries(3): the loop runs for j = 1, 2, 3
jj / (j + 1)in real arithmeticas int divisionsum
11 / 20.500
22 / 30.66700
33 / 40.7500

Then one sentence: "for any i, every term j/(j+1) has j < j+1, so integer division gives 0 every time; therefore sumSeries returns 0 for 3, 4, 5 and 7 alike." That sentence is the answer to all four values, and it is worth more than four traced tables.

Q2 c · dry run the subtraction loop · 4 MARKS

The question asks for the output of each iteration and the final output, which is a specific instruction: it wants the table, not just the number.

Dry run · x = x - nums[i], starting from nums[0]
nums = {2, 4, 6, 8}, and x starts at nums[0] = 2

exam.answer:
Q4 a · describe decision making, looping and branching · 3 MARKS

Model answer. These are the three families of control structure (Unit 4.1): the statements that decide which code runs and how often, rather than doing the work themselves.

  1. Decision-making. Choosing between paths by testing a condition, so that some code runs and some does not: if, if-else, the if-else ladder, and switch.
  2. Looping (iteration). Repeating a block while a condition holds: for, while and do-while. The do-while is the one that always runs at least once, because it tests at the bottom.
  3. Branching (jumping). Transferring control out of the normal flow: break leaves a loop or a switch case, continue skips to the next iteration, and return leaves the method entirely.

Where the marks are: name the actual keywords. "Looping means repeating" is the idea; "for, while, do-while, and do-while tests at the bottom so it runs at least once" is the answer. Units 4.1 to 4.7.

exam.answer:
Q4 b · debug the while loop · 3 MARKS

The paper prints that as a bare fragment. To put it through a real compiler it needs a class and a main around it, so that is what is added below, and nothing else is touched. Every fault you are about to list is the paper's own:

public class WhileDebugBroken {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int count = 1        float output = "";        while(count <=5); {            output = output + count + " ";            Count        }        System.out.println(output);    }}
Compiler outputerror: ';' expected

The errors, listed.

  1. int count = 1 has no semicolon.
  2. float output = ""; is the wrong type. A float is a number; "" is text. They are not interchangeable and Java will not convert one to the other. Fix: String output = "";
  3. while(count <=5); has a stray semicolon. This is the one worth the mark. That semicolon is the loop body: an empty statement. The block below it then runs once, on its own, as an ordinary block. Since count never changes inside the empty body, the condition stays true forever and the program hangs.
  4. Count is not a statement. Wrong case (Java is case sensitive) and, even spelled right, count alone does nothing. Fix: count++; which is what stops the loop.
Trap · The semicolon that eats the loop body

while (condition); and for (...); are both legal Java. The semicolon is an empty statement, and an empty statement is a perfectly good loop body. So the compiler says nothing at all.

What you wrote:

while (count <= 5); { ... }

What Java read:

while (count <= 5) { }   then, separately,   { ... }

The braces you meant as the body became a free-floating block that runs once, after the loop finishes. Except the loop never finishes, because nothing inside an empty body can change count.

This exact trap appears twice on this paper: here, and again in Q6 C as for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++);. The examiner is not being subtle about how much they want you to notice it. Whenever a loop misbehaves, look at the character immediately after the closing bracket. Unit 4.5.

Code · q4 b corrected · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class WhileDebug {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int count = 1;        String output = "";        while (count <= 5) {            output = output + count + " ";            count++;        }        System.out.println(output);    }}
Output1 2 3 4 5

There is a trailing space after the 5, because the loop appends count + " " every time including the last. Harmless, and worth writing down if you are asked for the output exactly.

exam.answer:
Q6 a · snippets for the three loop types · 3 MARKS

Part iii is the one being marked. A do-while whose condition is false still runs once, and "print 10 once" is the cleanest possible demonstration of that. Choose a condition that is false immediately, and the body still prints.

Code · q6 a · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class ThreeLoopTypes {    public static void main(String[] args) {        // i. a for loop printing 1 to 5        for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {            System.out.print(i + " ");        }        System.out.println();        // ii. a while loop printing 5 down to 1        int j = 5;        while (j >= 1) {            System.out.print(j + " ");            j--;        }        System.out.println();        // iii. a do-while printing only 10, once        int k = 10;        do {            System.out.print(k + " ");            k++;        } while (k <= 10);        System.out.println();    }}
Output1 2 3 4 5
5 4 3 2 1
10

In the do-while, k is 10, the body prints it, k becomes 11, and while (k <= 10) is false, so it stops. The body ran once before the condition was ever looked at, which is the whole difference between do-while and while. Write it as a while with the same condition and nothing prints at all. Unit 4.5.

exam.answer:
Q6 c · debug evenfinder · 4 MARKS
Compiler outputerror: ';' expected

The errors, listed.

  1. main(String args) is not main. It must be String[] args. Without the brackets it is an ordinary method that the JVM will not recognise as the entry point.
  2. printEven(10.0) has no semicolon.
  3. 10.0 is a double. The method takes an int, and Java will not narrow a double to an int on its own, because that loses information (Unit 3.3). Fix: printEven(10);
  4. printEven(int) has no parameter name. Fix: printEven(int n), which is also why n "does not exist" three lines later.
  5. for (...); has a stray semicolon. The loop body is empty, so the if below is not in the loop. It runs once, after the loop, and it cannot even compile: i was declared in the for, so it is out of scope the moment the for ends.

Error 5 is Q4 B's stray semicolon again, on the same paper, in a for this time. The scope error is what gives it away here: when the compiler says "cannot find symbol: i" about a variable you can plainly see, the loop that declared it has already closed.

The output after correction: 0 2 4 6 8 10

Code · q6 c corrected · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class EvenFinder {    public static void main(String[] args) {        printEven(10);    }    public static void printEven(int n) {        for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {            if (i % 2 == 0) {                System.out.print(i + " ");            }        }        System.out.println();    }}
Output0 2 4 6 8 10

0 is even, and i <= n means 10 is included, so the answer starts at 0 and ends at 10. Both ends are worth checking: this is the rare loop where <= is correct, because n is a value to reach, not a length.

scenario.text:
[7.5 marks]D. Write a program that includes a method called hasEqualAdjacentPairs(int n) which:

i.    Returns true if the number n (a positive integer) contains at least two pairs of equal adjacent digits.

ii.   Returns false otherwise.

iii.  You must:

a.  Write the method hasEqualAdjacentPairs(int n)

b.  Write the main() method to test at least two cases

Example

•  112233 - true (pairs: 11, 22, 33). More than two adjacent pairs.

•  1223 - true (pairs: 22). Only one pair - return false

Reproduced exactly. The second example is self-contradictory as printed: it says "true" and then "return false". The rule in part i is the one to trust. This is discussed in the answer below.

exam.problem: Write your answer to the question above in your book first. It carries 7.5 marks, so write one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Q6 d · hasequaladjacentpairs · 7.5 MARKS

112233 → true (pairs: 11, 22, 33). More than two adjacent pairs.
1223 → true (pairs: 22). Only one pair → return false

Trap · The paper contradicts itself, and you must answer anyway

Read the second example again. It says "1223 - true" and then, in the same line, "Only one pair - return false". Both cannot be right.

The specification says "at least two pairs". 1223 has one pair, the 22. One is not at least two.

The correct return is false. The leading "true" is a slip of the pen.

The examiner's own explanation ("Only one pair") agrees with the specification, so the specification and the reasoning outvote the stray word. This book shows you the paper exactly as printed and tells you what is true, and it never quietly corrects a source (compare the six errors in Module 3, which come from this course's own slides).

What to do in the hall. Do not agonise, and do not answer the typo. Implement the specification, and write one line saying why: "1223 has only one adjacent pair, so by the stated rule of at least two pairs the method returns false; the 'true' in the example appears to be a typographical error." That sentence costs ten seconds and it protects you whichever way the marking scheme reads, because it proves the answer was a decision and not a mistake.

MEMORY HOOK: when a question contradicts itself, follow the specification and say that you did.

Code · q6 d, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class AdjacentPairs {    // i/ii. true when n has AT LEAST TWO pairs of equal adjacent digits.    public static boolean hasEqualAdjacentPairs(int n) {        int pairs = 0;        int previous = n % 10;        n = n / 10;        while (n > 0) {            int current = n % 10;            if (current == previous) {                pairs++;            }            previous = current;            n = n / 10;        }        return pairs >= 2;    }    // iii b. main testing more than the two cases the question asks for    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] tests = {112233, 1223, 1122, 111, 123, 7, 122333};        for (int t : tests) {            System.out.println(t + " -> " + hasEqualAdjacentPairs(t));        }    }}
Output112233 -> true
1223 -> false
1122 -> true
111 -> true
123 -> false
7 -> false
122333 -> true

The paper asks for at least two test cases; there are seven, and each earns its place. 112233 and 1223 are the paper's own. 1122 is the boundary: exactly two pairs, so exactly true. 111 asks what a triple counts as. 123 has no pairs and 7 has no adjacent digits at all, so the loop never runs and pairs stays 0.

Must memorise · Compare adjacent digits by remembering the last one

Take the last digit before the loop and call it previous. Then each turn: take the new current, compare it with previous, and make current the new previous.

That is the whole technique, and it is the same % 10 and / 10 pair as Q6 A on the 2025/26 paper. The only new idea is carrying one value forward so that each digit can see its neighbour. You never need the digits in an array; you need exactly one of them remembered.

111 gives two pairs, not one. The digits are compared in overlapping pairs: positions 1-2 and 2-3. The middle 1 belongs to both. If you think a triple should count once, that is a different specification, and this one does not say so: it says pairs of equal adjacent digits, and 111 contains two of them.

MEMORY HOOK: to compare neighbours, remember one. Peel a digit, compare, then let it become the memory for the next.
